title: English Language mock paper (4EB1 style) and timing card
subject: English Language
source: Written for english-language/y11 lesson 37 (Mock week paper (4EB1 style, 3 hours) and timing card (pupil PDF))
intro: Answer ALL questions in Sections A and B, and ONE question in Section C. Read the questions before the texts.

blocks.h: Timing card (school guide for a 9:00 start)

passage.title: Text One: Night Train
paras: The train was supposed to leave at nine. At ten past, a guard walked the length of the platform, shrugged at nobody in particular and went back inside. I sat on my rucksack and ate the last of my bread, which tasted faintly of the bag it had travelled in.

When we finally moved, it was with a jolt that sent a suitcase sliding into my knees. The carriage was full of strangers settling in for the night: a grandmother unpacking an entire meal from a single tin, two students arguing softly over a map, a man in a suit who removed his tie, folded it like a letter and slept at once.

Outside, the city thinned into warehouses, then fields, then nothing but darkness pressed against the glass. Every so often a level crossing flashed past: a red light, a ringing bell, a single car waiting with its headlights on, and then the dark again. I tried to read and gave up. The rhythm of the wheels was saying something I could not quite make out.

At some point in the night the grandmother tapped my arm and held out a piece of flatbread wrapped in a napkin. We had no language in common. I said thank you in mine; she nodded in hers. It was the best thing I ate on the whole journey.

I woke to grey light and mountains. The students were asleep on each other's shoulders; the man in the suit was retying his tie. Nobody said goodbye when we arrived. But I have never since sat on a train without looking round the carriage and wondering who, tonight, will share their bread.
passage.source: Teacher-written for TGA as an unseen text for the mock (the writer is invented).

questions.q: From paragraph 1, what does the narrator eat while waiting?
From paragraph 2, give one of the passengers the narrator describes.
questions.a: Any one: a grandmother with a meal in a tin; two students arguing over a map; a man in a suit

questions.q: How does the writer use language and structure to show the experience of the night journey? Support your answer with examples from the text.
questions.a: Language: the darkness 'pressed against the glass'; the rhythm of the wheels 'saying something'; the list at the level crossing; humour ('shrugged at nobody in particular'). Structure: chronological from delay to arrival; the shift from strangers to the shared bread; the circular ending that looks to future journeys. Reward analysis of effects. Level 4 (8-10) perceptive analysis of language and structure; Level 3 (5-7) clear; Level 2 (3-4) some comment; Level 1 (1-2) simple.

passage.title: Text Two: Hints for the Railway Traveller
paras: The railway has made us a nation of travellers, and it is a strange thing that so many who would never set out on a walk without stout boots will enter a railway carriage with no preparation whatever.

Let the traveller, then, arrive in good time. The train waits for no man, and the porter who is hurried is a porter who drops things. Let him carry his ticket where he can find it, and his money where others cannot.

Once seated, he should choose his companions' conversation as carefully as his seat. The gentleman who tells you his whole history before the first station will tell yours to the next passenger before the second. Courtesy costs nothing; confidences may cost a great deal.

As to comfort: a rug for the knees, a book of moderate weight, and some plain food against delay. The refreshment rooms at the larger stations are tolerable; those at the smaller are best left to the imagination.

Above all, let him remember that the railway, for all its speed, has not abolished the old virtues of the road. Patience, good humour and a willingness to help a fellow traveller will carry a man further than any express.
passage.source: Teacher-written for TGA in a nineteenth-century style, as an unseen text for the mock.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why should the traveller arrive in good time?
questions.a: The train waits for no one / a hurried porter drops things

questions.q: Give two things the writer suggests taking for comfort.
questions.a: Any two: a rug for the knees; a book of moderate weight; some plain food against delay

questions.q: How does the writer use language and structure to give advice to the railway traveller?
questions.a: Imperatives and 'let him' commands give authority; humorous aphorisms ('Courtesy costs nothing; confidences may cost a great deal'); contrast of large and small refreshment rooms; structure from arrival to journey to 'Above all', ending on moral virtues. Levels as Question 3.

questions.q: Compare how the writers of Text One and Text Two present their ideas and perspectives about travelling by train. Support your answer with detailed reference to both texts.
questions.a: Both value patience and fellow travellers: Text One through the personal moment of shared bread, Text Two through general advice to help 'a fellow traveller'. Differences: modern first-person memoir and reflection against nineteenth-century instructional, authoritative voice; Text One open to strangers, Text Two cautious about confidences. Reward integrated comparison and methods. Level 5 (13-15) perceptive, integrated; Level 4 (10-12) clear and detailed; Level 3 (7-9) clear; Level 2 (4-6) some; Level 1 (1-3) simple.

questions.q: Your school magazine is publishing a guide for students making their first long journey by train. Write the article. You should: explain what can make long journeys difficult; give advice on preparing and travelling; suggest how a journey can be more than just getting from one place to another. Use ideas from BOTH texts, in your own words.
questions.a: Reward adapted ideas from both texts (delays, food, rugs or comfort, choosing seats and company, kindness of strangers, patience) and a suitable article form for students: headline, introduction, paragraphs for each bullet, conclusion. AO1 (10) ideas adapted; AO4 (12) form, audience, purpose; AO5 (8) accuracy. Check level descriptors against the current Pearson sample assessment materials.

blocks.h: Section C: writing (30 marks). Answer ONE question.

questions.q: Choose one: (9) 'Travel is wasted on the young.' Discuss. (10) Write a story called 'The Wrong Stop'. (11) Describe a busy station at dawn.
questions.a: AO4 (20): a controlled, crafted response suited to the task type (discursive: both sides and a judgement; narrative: shape, tension, change; descriptive: one place, senses, zoom). AO5 (10): range of sentences and vocabulary, accurate spelling and punctuation.

markScheme.a: Mark allocations follow the paper at a glance taught in lesson 25 (Q1, Q2, Q4 1 mark each, Q5 2, Q3 and Q6 10 each, Q7 15, Q8 30, Section C 30). Check the level descriptors against the current Pearson 4EB1 sample assessment materials before marking.
